title: You Took a Business Loan and Now Nobody Can Show Where the Money Went
description: A loan landed months ago and the money is gone into ordinary spending. Now the balance, the spending, and the books cannot tell the same story.

blocks.text: This article is general information about business recordkeeping, not tax or legal advice for a specific business.

The day the loan funded felt like relief. The deposit was large and unmistakable in the account, and for a moment the pressure that had been building for months eased. Rent was current, a supplier who had been waiting was paid, payroll felt less tight, and the business could breathe again. Nobody thought of the deposit as the start of a story that would have to be told, in full, months later. It felt like money that had arrived to do a job, and then it simply went to work.

That is exactly how it disappears as a separate thing. A loan does not stay in an account wearing a label. It mixes with customer payments, with the balance that was already there, with the ordinary flow of a busy month. It pays for things that look, in the bank feed, exactly like things paid from any other money. A parts order, a repair, a tax payment, a week of wages. Each payment is real, each one was needed, and none of them, on their own, announces that loan money was the source. By the second month, the loan is no longer a pile of money anyone can point to. It is a balance owed, on one side of the books, and a history of ordinary spending, on the other, with no clear thread tying the two together.
The trouble does not arrive while the money is being spent. It arrives when someone asks, calmly and reasonably, where it went.
The question sounds simple, and that is the problem

A lender, an accountant, or a partner asking about a loan is not asking a trick question. The loan agreement exists, the funding date exists, the amount exists. What they want is the middle of the story. The money came in, it was used for the business, the business still owes the balance, and the records should show that arc without guesswork.

In too many businesses, they cannot. The books may show the loan as income in the month it landed, which makes that month look stronger than it was. Or they may show the deposit and then lose it, with repayments recorded as ordinary expenses, which makes later months look weaker and stranger than they were. Or the loan may sit correctly as a liability while the spending it funded is scattered across categories with no notes, no receipts kept together, and no way for a reader who was not there to follow it.

The IRS recordkeeping guidance makes the underlying expectation plain. Businesses need records that support income, deductions, and credits, and supporting documents for purchases and expenses should identify the payee, the amount, proof of payment, and the date, along with what was bought. A loan tests that expectation in a particular way, because the most important fact about the money, that it was borrowed and must be repaid, is invisible in a bank deposit alone. A deposit from customers and a deposit from a lender can look identical to anyone reading the account later. Only the records around them carry the difference.

When those surrounding records are thin, the conversation changes tone. The owner knows the money went into the business. The owner was there, remembers the tight weeks, remembers what felt urgent. But the person asking was not there, and their job is not to grade intentions. Their job is to read what can be shown.
Ordinary spending is the hardest spending to trace

There is a quiet irony owners feel sharply in this moment. If the loan had bought one large piece of equipment, the story would be easier to follow. One invoice, one payment, one asset that still stands in the building as evidence. Most loans do not live that cleanly. They fund the ordinary life of a business that was short on cash, and ordinary life is dozens of payments, in familiar amounts, to familiar names.

Rent paid from loan money looks like rent paid from any money. Payroll run in a loan funded week looks like every other payroll. Inventory bought to keep shelves full, fuel, insurance, a contractor who had to be paid before a job could finish, each charge blends into the pattern around it. Months later, reconstructing which dollars were borrowed dollars is not merely difficult. In a shared account, it is a question the records were never set up to answer, and memory fills the gap with a confidence that fades under follow up questions.

That fading matters because the amounts rarely line up neatly by then. Part of the loan may still be sitting in the account, mixed with newer receipts. Part may have covered an overdraft or a credit card balance that itself covered earlier spending, so the trail doubles back on itself. Interest and fees add their own entries, small enough to ignore in a busy week and large enough, over a year, to make balances quietly disagree.

The owner ends up telling three versions without meaning to. The bank tells one, the loan statement tells another, and the books tell a third. None of them is dishonest. They simply were never made to agree while the story was still fresh.
The balance owed starts to feel like an argument

A loan that cannot be traced does not stay a private confusion. It follows the business into rooms where trust is being priced. An accountant preparing a return needs to know that the deposit was not revenue, because treating borrowed money as earned money distorts the year and everything built on it. A lender considering a second loan, a refinance, or a line increase reads the first loan as a test of stewardship, and a file that cannot show the use of funds asks that lender to extend more trust than the paper supports. A partner or co owner who was not part of the spending decisions hears explanations where they expected records, and even a fair explanation can start to sound like a story being built after the fact.

Tax time sharpens all of it. The federal baseline in the IRS guidance is that records supporting a return are kept until the limitations period for that return expires, generally three years from filing, longer in some cases, with employment tax records kept at least four years. A loan that spans a year end, as most do, lives inside that window on both sides of the calendar. The deposit in one year, the spending across two, the repayments still running. If the paper behind any leg of that journey is missing, the weakness is not contained to the month of the loan. It spreads across every return and report that touched the money.

Owners often describe the feeling as unfair, and in one sense it is. The money was not wasted in secret. It kept a real business running through real obligations, and the people who were paid could confirm it. But a loan is, by its nature, someone else money inside the business for a while, and that fact raises the standard for what the records need to show. Customer revenue belongs to the story the business tells about what it earned. Borrowed money belongs to a story about what it was trusted with. Confusing the two, even by neglect, is the point where a routine deposit becomes a credibility problem.
What remains when the trail goes cold

By the time anyone sits down to untangle it, the business is usually paying for the same loan twice. Once in the monthly payment itself, and again in the hours spent searching old statements, in the accountant time billed to reconstruct a year, in the delay while a lender waits for an answer that should have taken minutes. The deepest cost is the moment an owner realizes they cannot fully account for a significant amount of money that passed through their own business, and that everyone in the room can see it.

That moment rarely comes from one careless act. It comes from a funded loan treated, in the rush of relief, as if the deposit were the end of the paperwork instead of the beginning of it. The spending that followed was legitimate, and that legitimacy is exactly what let each payment pass without a second thought. Legitimate spending still needs a trail when the money was borrowed. Without one, legitimacy is a memory, and memory is not a record anyone else can rely on.

The loan will be repaid on schedule or it will not, and the statement will keep arriving with its calm, exact balance. The open question is whether their own books can stand next to that statement and tell the same story, in the same amounts, for the same months. When they cannot, the debt is not the heaviest part of the loan anymore. The missing story is.
This article is general information about business recordkeeping, not tax or legal advice for a specific business.

title: The Year Ends With Gift Cards Sold, Money Collected, and Work Still Owed in January
description: Holiday gift card sales feel like a strong finish to the year. The cash is in, but the work is still owed in January, and the books feel it later.

blocks.text: This article is general information about business recordkeeping, not tax or legal advice for a specific business.

December is the one month when customers happily pay for work they do not want yet. A gift card is bought in a good mood, wrapped or emailed, and celebrated as a thoughtful present, while the appointment, the meal, the service, or the goods it promises sit weeks or months in the future. For the business on the other side of the counter, the sale feels wonderful in the moment. The register is busy, the deposits are strong, and a hard year appears to be ending on a high note that everyone earned.

That feeling is real, and it is also incomplete. The money has arrived, but the business has not finished with it. Every card sold and not yet redeemed is a promise walking around in someone else pocket, waiting to come back at a time the business does not choose. When January arrives, quieter, colder, with rent and payroll at their full size, those promises start returning one by one, asking for labor, time, and product, without bringing any new money in with them.

If the books treated December as if all of that cash were already earned, the new year opens with a distortion nobody intended, and the owner is left wondering why a strong December produced such a strained January.
Cash in hand is not the same as work completed

The confusion is understandable because, from the bank account point of view, a gift card sale looks like any other sale. Money lands, the day total rises, the month closes stronger. Nothing in a deposit announces that part of it belongs to work still owed. Only the records around the sale carry that fact, the card number, the amount, the date sold, and later, the date and amount redeemed.

The IRS recordkeeping guidance stresses that a business needs records that support the income it reports, along with gross receipts, sales records, and supporting documents that show what was received and when. Gift cards stretch that discipline across a year boundary. The receipt happens in one year, the service or goods are delivered in another, and a record that only captures the cash will misdescribe both years. December looks richer than the work it actually completed. January looks poorer, carrying the cost of fulfilling promises while showing little of the money that paid for them.

Owners feel this first as a mood, before they see it as a number. January staff are busy redeeming, the schedule may even look healthy, and yet the account does not grow the way a busy schedule should make it grow. The work is real and the money is not new. A team that celebrated December as a breakthrough month starts the year feeling behind, without any single mistake they can point to.

That gap in understanding hardens when some cards are redeemed in part, some in full, some for more than the card value with a second payment added, and some not at all for many months. Each path leaves a slightly different trace in the sales system, in the card processor reports, and in the bank. A reader later, an accountant closing the year, a buyer looking at seasonal performance, a partner trying to understand December, has to reconcile all of those traces into one honest account of what was sold, what was delivered, and what is still owed to customers holding unredeemed balances.
A liability that walks out the door in an envelope

Most obligations of a business stay visible. A vendor bill sits in a pile or a system, a loan statement arrives every month, payroll announces itself on a schedule. An unredeemed gift card is quieter. It leaves the building in an envelope, a wallet, or an inbox, and the business may not hear from it again until the least convenient week of winter, or the following holiday season, or never within the period anyone was watching.

That quietness is what lets the balance owed to card holders drift out of the books entirely. If no one kept a running record that the business could trust, the amount still owed becomes an estimate offered from memory, and memory, in a business that sold cards across busy counters, holiday events, and online orders at the same time, is not a reliable ledger. Promotional cards given away in a marketing push mix with cards that were paid for. Cards sold through a third party platform settle on a different schedule than cards sold in person. A card that was refunded, replaced, or reissued can appear twice in one system and once in another.

None of this requires carelessness at the level of intent. Holiday selling is fast, seasonal help is new, and the line at the counter rewards speed over documentation. The problems are created in small, forgivable moments, a card activated without its sale being fully recorded, a manual adjustment made to keep the line moving, an online sale that landed in a report nobody checked against the bank. Each one is minor in December. Together, they decide whether the business actually knows what it owes its own customers when the year turns.

There is a customer trust side to it as well. A holder who presents a card and is told the balance cannot be verified, or shows as less than they believe, experiences that moment as the business questioning them. The record failure becomes a service failure, in public, at the counter, months after the original sale was celebrated.
The year gets closed on a number that was never quite true

Year end is when the distortion stops being a feeling and becomes a filing. A return, a financial statement, or a simple year in review built on December cash alone will overstate what that year earned from work completed and understate what the next year still has to deliver. The federal recordkeeping baseline is that records supporting income and deductions are kept until the limitations period for the return expires, generally three years from filing, and employment tax records at least four years, so a weak gift card record does not fade quickly. It sits inside the closed year, available to confuse every comparison built on top of it.

Owners comparing years feel it without naming it. One December looks like the best month the business ever had, the next December looks like a decline, when part of the difference is only when promises were counted. A lender or buyer reading those months sees momentum where there was really an obligation building, and sees a soft January where there was really work being honored. Decisions about staffing, about whether the holiday push worked, about whether to repeat a promotion, get made on a story the cash told too early.

The businesses that sell the most cards are often the ones most exposed, because the amounts are large enough to matter and the volume is large enough to outrun informal tracking. A handful of cards can live in an owner memory. Hundreds of cards, across locations, staff, and platforms, cannot. At that scale the question is no longer whether the money was collected. It plainly was. The question is whether the business can show, card by card and month by month, how much of that collected money has been earned by work actually done, and how much is still a promise outstanding.

When it cannot, January tells the truth that December deferred. The appointments arrive, the redemptions arrive, the costs arrive, and the revenue that was supposed to accompany them is already spent, counted, and closed in a year that has ended. Nothing was stolen and nothing was wasted. The year simply called money earned before the business had finished earning it, and the new year inherits the work without the recognition.

That is the quiet weight of a gift card season recorded only by its cash. The cards were sold as a sign that customers trusted the business enough to pay in advance. Honoring that trust, on paper as well as at the counter, is what separates a strong December from a December that only looked strong until January asked for the rest of the story.
This article is general information about business recordkeeping, not tax or legal advice for a specific business.

title: Your Sales Report and Your Bank Deposits Never Agree, and Nobody Knows Which One Is Right
description: The sales report says one number, the bank says another, and the gap grows every month. When neither can be trusted, every decision built on them wobbles.

blocks.text: This article is general information about business recordkeeping, not tax or legal advice for a specific business.

It starts as a small difference nobody has time for. The sales report for the week says one amount, the deposits that reached the bank say another, slightly lower, slightly later, close enough that a busy owner rounds it off in their head and moves on. There is a line at the counter, a delivery at the back door, a payroll deadline at the end of the week. The gap is noted the way a strange noise in an old truck is noted, real, familiar, and postponed.

Then a month closes and the gap is still there, larger, and now it has company. Some days agree almost exactly. Some days are off by amounts that match nothing obvious. A refund appears in one place and not the other. A busy Saturday shows up in the bank on Tuesday, split into two deposits, minus amounts nobody labeled. By the time the accountant or the owner sits down to ask a simple question, what did we actually sell last month, the business has two answers, and no honest way to choose between them.

That is the point where a routine annoyance becomes something heavier. A business can survive a lot of uncertainty, but it cannot plan, price, borrow, or file with confidence on numbers its own owner no longer trusts.
Two systems that were never describing the same moment

Part of the confusion is that the sales report and the bank account are not, and never were, measuring the same event at the same time. The sales system records the moment a customer paid, or promised, or tapped a card at the counter. The bank records the moment money actually arrived, cleared, and settled, often days later, often batched with other days, often reduced before it lands.

Card payments make the distance widest. A day of card sales may settle in pieces, with processing amounts taken out along the way, chargebacks or adjustments arriving weeks after the original sale, and weekend sales landing together on a weekday morning. Cash has its own drift, deposited in person, sometimes held a day, sometimes combined, sometimes short in ways that may be error, loss, or a counting mistake nobody documented. Online orders, third party platforms, and gift card redemptions each add another report, another timing pattern, another version of the same week.

The IRS recordkeeping guidance expects a business to keep records that support gross receipts and income, with supporting documents such as sales records, deposit information, invoices, and receipts that allow income to be verified. That expectation is not satisfied by having two totals that disagree and a general feeling that they are probably close. Close is not a record. When the supporting trail between a sale and its deposit cannot be followed, the business does not have a small formatting problem. It has a gap in the very evidence its income rests on.

Owners usually know, in general terms, why the numbers differ. Fees, timing, refunds, they can name the categories in a sentence. What they cannot do, month after month, is show it, sale day by sale day, in amounts that tie out. Naming a reason in general and proving a specific difference are different things, and the distance between them is where trust in the numbers quietly dies.
The gap becomes the place where real problems hide

A persistent unexplained difference is dangerous not only because it is unexplained. It is dangerous because, once everyone accepts that sales and deposits never quite agree, almost anything can hide inside that acceptance. A genuine error, a missed deposit, a duplicate entry, a sale recorded twice, a refund processed twice, a day of cash that never reached the bank, each one arrives looking exactly like the normal drift everyone has learned to ignore.

Staff learn it too. If the standard is that the numbers are always off by something, then being off by something more stops raising questions. A closing count that should have prompted a second look gets signed because yesterday was off as well. A manager explaining a shortage has the perfect cover, not because they invented it, but because the business built it, week by week, by tolerating a gap it never explained.

The owner feels the cost in a different way, in decisions that never quite land. Was last month actually better than the month before, or did a settlement calendar just bunch three weekends into one deposit window. Did a promotion work, or did the report count redemptions and prepayments as if they were new demand. Can the business afford another hire on the strength of a sales trend that the bank never confirmed. Every one of those questions deserves a single trusted number, and instead the owner is handed two, with a shrug between them.

At tax time, and in any serious review, the shrug stops working. Records supporting a return are expected to be kept until the limitations period for that return expires, generally three years from filing under the federal baseline, with employment tax records kept at least four years. A year built on unreconciled months does not become more solid with age. It becomes harder to reconstruct, as staff turn over, processor reports age out of easy reach, and the small daily reasons behind each difference fade from everyone memory at once.
Nobody trusts either number, so everybody keeps their own

The most telling symptom is what people inside the business start to do. The owner keeps a mental number, based on feel and the bank balance. A manager keeps a spreadsheet, based on the sales system and their own adjustments. The bookkeeper or accountant works from deposits, because deposits at least reached the bank. Each person is acting reasonably, and together they have created a business with three versions of its own performance, used in three different conversations, none of them able to correct the others.

Meetings absorb the difference without resolving it. A good month is celebrated on the sales report and questioned on the bank statement in the same breath. A bad month is excused the other way around. Over time the argument stops being about what the business did and becomes about which report to believe this time, a debate that can be won by whoever is speaking and lost again the following week.

Outside the business, the cost is plainer. A lender reading financials that do not tie to deposits sees risk where the owner sees a timing quirk. An accountant asked to certify, prepare, or simply stand behind a set of numbers built on an open gap has to price that uncertainty, qualify that work, or spend billable hours rebuilding months that should have closed cleanly the first time. A buyer, if one ever looks, will believe the lower provable number and discount the rest, because buyers always trust the trail that can be shown over the total that can only be asserted.

None of this means money was lost, or that anyone acted in bad faith. In most businesses living with this gap, the great majority of the difference is ordinary, explainable, and boring, if it were ever actually explained at the time it occurred. The harm is that, unexamined, ordinary and serious differences become indistinguishable, and a business that cannot tell them apart has lost control of the first fact it needs, how much it truly sold and received.

A sales report should be a promise the bank can keep, a day or a few days later, in amounts that can be followed from one to the other without faith or folklore. When that thread is intact, a difference is just information, quickly understood. When it is broken in a dozen small places, every month end becomes a small investigation, every decision carries a discount for doubt, and the owner is left running a business whose own numbers need an apology before they can be used.

The deposits will keep landing and the reports will keep printing. The question that decides whether either of them is useful is whether anyone can stand between them, month after month, and show exactly why they differ, down to the last ordinary fee and the last late settlement. Until that showing is possible, the business does not have two sources of truth. It has none it can fully rely on, and it feels that absence every time a real decision needs a real number.
This article is general information about business recordkeeping, not tax or legal advice for a specific business.
